acceptedAnswer.text: Recursion in Java is a programming technique where a method calls itself directly or indirectly to solve a problem by breaking it down into smaller subproblems of the same type. Every recursive method must have a base case (a condition where the method stops calling itself) and a recursive case (where the method calls itself with a modified argument moving towards the base case). Without a base case, recursion leads to infinite calls and a StackOverflowError.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between recursion and iteration in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Recursion solves a problem by having a function call itself, using the call stack to maintain state, and is more natural for problems with recursive structure (trees, graphs, divide-and-conquer). Iteration solves problems using loops (for, while) and is generally more memory-efficient because it doesn't consume stack frames. Recursion can cause StackOverflowError for very deep calls; iteration does not. Iteration is usually faster due to no method-call overhead. However, recursive solutions are often shorter and more readable for problems like tree traversal, Tower of Hanoi, and DFS.

mainEntity.name: What is a base case in recursion?

acceptedAnswer.text: A base case is the condition in a recursive method that stops further recursive calls and returns a direct result without calling itself again. Every correct recursive method MUST have at least one base case. Without it, the method calls itself infinitely, consuming stack memory until a StackOverflowError occurs. Example for factorial: 'if (n == 0) return 1;' — when n reaches 0, no further recursion happens and the value 1 is returned directly.

mainEntity.name: What is tail recursion in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Tail recursion is a special form of recursion where the recursive call is the LAST operation in the method — no pending computation waits after the recursive call returns. Example: 'return factorial(n-1, acc * n)' is tail-recursive because nothing happens after the recursive call. Tail recursion is significant because compilers/runtimes can optimize it into a loop (tail call optimization), eliminating stack frame buildup. IMPORTANT: The Java JVM does NOT automatically optimize tail recursion, so tail-recursive Java methods still risk StackOverflowError for large inputs — unlike languages like Scala or Haskell.

mainEntity.name: What causes StackOverflowError in Java recursion?

acceptedAnswer.text: StackOverflowError occurs in Java recursion when the call stack runs out of memory due to too many nested recursive calls. Each recursive call creates a new stack frame on the JVM's call stack. The default JVM stack size is typically 512KB–1MB, which allows roughly 1,000–10,000 recursive calls depending on frame size. Causes: (1) Missing base case — infinite recursion. (2) Base case never reached — e.g., factorial(-1) with base case n==0. (3) Input too large — e.g., recursive Fibonacci for n=100,000. Solutions: add/fix base case, use iteration, or increase stack size with -Xss JVM flag.

sections.title: What is Recursion in Java?

blocks.text: Recursion in Java is a programming technique where a method calls itself — either directly or indirectly — to solve a problem. The core idea is divide and conquer: break a large problem into a smaller subproblem of the same type, solve the smaller version, and combine results. Recursion continues until it reaches a base case — a condition where no further calling is needed and a direct answer is returned.

Recursion is not just a coding trick — it is a fundamental problem-solving paradigm. Many real-world structures are inherently recursive: a file system is a folder containing files and other folders; an HTML DOM is an element containing other elements; a company org-chart is a person managing other persons. Algorithms like merge sort, quick sort, depth-first search, and tree traversal are expressed most naturally using recursion.

In Java, recursion is implemented through method calls. Each time a method calls itself, a new stack frame is pushed onto the JVM's call stack, holding local variables and the return address. When the base case is reached, stack frames are popped one by one — each returning its value to the caller above it — until the original call returns the final answer.

blocks.title: 🔑 Java Recursion at a Glance
blocks.text: Every recursive method in Java must have: (1) A BASE CASE — a condition that terminates recursion and returns a value directly. (2) A RECURSIVE CASE — where the method calls itself with a smaller/simpler argument, progressing toward the base case. (3) PROGRESS — each recursive call MUST move closer to the base case. Without these three, recursion leads to infinite calls and StackOverflowError.

sections.title: How Recursion Works — The Call Stack

blocks.text: Understanding recursion requires understanding the call stack. The JVM maintains a stack (LIFO — Last In, First Out) where each method call creates a stack frame. A stack frame contains: local variables, parameters, and the return address (where to continue after this method finishes). When a recursive method calls itself, a new stack frame is pushed. When it returns, that frame is popped and control returns to the previous frame.

items.title: Winding Phase (Call Phase)
items.text: Each recursive call pushes a new frame onto the call stack. Variables are initialized and the method body executes until it hits the next recursive call. This continues until the BASE CASE is reached — no more recursive calls are made. The stack grows upward with each call.

items.title: Unwinding Phase (Return Phase)
items.text: Once the base case returns a value, the stack begins to UNWIND. Each frame receives the return value from the frame below it, computes its own result, and returns it to the frame above. This continues until the original call receives the final answer and the stack is empty again.

items.title: Stack Frame Contents
items.text: Each stack frame holds: (1) Method parameters (e.g., n in factorial(n)). (2) Local variables declared inside the method. (3) The return address — where execution resumes in the CALLING method. (4) A reference to the return value. Larger local state = larger frames = fewer recursive calls before StackOverflowError.

sections.title: Base Case & Recursive Case — The Two Pillars of Recursion

blocks.text: Every correct recursive method in Java is built on two essential components: the base case and the recursive case. Missing either one — or getting them wrong — results in either a StackOverflowError (infinite recursion) or an incorrect answer. Think of the base case as the exit door and the recursive case as the staircase leading down to it.

blocks.title: ⚠️ The Convergence Requirement
blocks.text: Every recursive call MUST move closer to the base case — this is called convergence. factorial(n-1) converges because n decreases by 1 each time. If your recursive call does NOT change the argument in a way that moves toward the base case — for example, factorial(n) calling factorial(n) — you have infinite recursion regardless of the base case. Always verify: 'Will every possible input eventually reach the base case?'

sections.title: Types of Recursion in Java — Overview

blocks.text: Java supports several forms of recursion, each with distinct characteristics in terms of structure, call stack behaviour, and ideal use cases. Understanding these types helps you choose the right recursive pattern for a given problem and recognize them in existing code.

items.title: Direct Recursion
items.text: A method calls ITSELF directly. Most common form. Example: factorial() calling factorial(). Clear to read, trace, and debug. Call chain: A → A → A → ... → base case.

items.title: Indirect (Mutual) Recursion
items.text: Method A calls Method B, which calls Method A back — forming a recursive cycle through multiple methods. Less common but used in parsers and state machines. Call chain: A → B → A → B → ... → base case.

items.title: Tail Recursion
items.text: The recursive call is the LAST operation — no pending computation after it returns. Structurally optimizable (though JVM does not auto-optimize). Accumulator parameter pattern. Example: factorial(n, accumulator).

items.title: Head Recursion
items.text: The recursive call is the FIRST operation — processing happens AFTER the recursive call returns (during unwinding). Contrast with tail recursion. Behaviour: processes values in reverse order during unwinding.

items.title: Tree Recursion
items.text: A method makes MORE THAN ONE recursive call per invocation, creating a branching call tree. Example: Fibonacci calls fibonacci(n-1) AND fibonacci(n-2). Exponential time complexity without memoization — O(2ⁿ) for naive Fibonacci.

items.title: Nested Recursion
items.text: The argument to the recursive call is itself a recursive call: f(f(n-1)). Very rare. Ackermann function is a famous nested-recursive function. Extremely deep call stacks, rarely used in production Java code.

sections.title: Direct Recursion — Method Calls Itself

blocks.text: Direct recursion is the most common and straightforward form: a method calls itself by name within its own body. The call chain is linear: each invocation spawns exactly one recursive call, building up the stack until the base case is reached, then unwinding.

blocks.label: DirectRecursion.java
lines: // Example 2: Sum of first n natural numbers
public static double power(double base, int exp) {
return base * power(base, exp - 1);           // Recursive case

sections.title: Indirect (Mutual) Recursion — Methods Call Each Other

blocks.text: Indirect recursion (also called mutual recursion) occurs when method A calls method B, and method B calls method A back — forming a cycle through two or more methods. The chain continues until a base case in one of the methods terminates the cycle. This pattern appears in parsers, grammar processors, and certain state machines.

blocks.label: IndirectRecursion.java
lines: // Classic example: isEven and isOdd via mutual recursion
if (n == 0) return true;          // Base case: 0 is even
if (n == 0) return false;         // Base case: 0 is not odd
return isEven(n - 1);             // Delegates back to isEven
// isEven(4) → isOdd(3) → isEven(2) → isOdd(1) → isEven(0) → true
public static boolean isAllDigits(String s, int index) {
if (index == s.length()) return true;   // Base case: processed all chars
public static boolean isDigitChar(String s, int index) {
if (!Character.isDigit(s.charAt(index))) return false; // Base case: not a digit

blocks.title: ⚠️ Indirect Recursion — Harder to Debug
blocks.text: Indirect recursion is significantly harder to trace and debug than direct recursion because the call chain spans multiple methods. A missing base case or incorrect termination condition may not be obvious from looking at a single method. Always trace the full call chain manually for small inputs when working with mutual recursion. For complex scenarios, consider logging or using a debugger to watch the call stack.

sections.title: Tail Recursion — Last Operation is the Recursive Call

blocks.text: Tail recursion is a special form of recursion where the recursive call is the last operation performed in the method — nothing happens after the recursive call returns. The result of the recursive call is directly returned without any further computation. This is achieved by passing an accumulator parameter that builds the result as the recursion progresses (during winding), rather than during unwinding.

blocks.label: TailRecursion.java
lines: // ❌ NOT tail-recursive: multiplication happens AFTER recursive call returns
return n * factorialNonTail(n - 1); // 'n *' is pending — NOT tail call
// ✅ TAIL-RECURSIVE: recursive call is LAST — accumulator carries the result
public static long factorialTail(int n, long accumulator) {
if (n <= 1) return accumulator;              // Base case: return built-up result
return factorialTail(n - 1, accumulator * n); // LAST operation — tail call
public static int sumTail(int n, int accumulator) {
return sumTail(n - 1, accumulator + n);  // Tail call
public static long fibTail(int n, long prev, long curr) {
return fibTail(n - 1, curr, prev + curr); // Tail call

blocks.title: ⚠️ Java JVM Does NOT Optimize Tail Recursion
blocks.text: Unlike Scala, Haskell, or Kotlin, the standard Java JVM does NOT perform Tail Call Optimization (TCO). Tail-recursive Java methods still create a new stack frame for every call, so they can still cause StackOverflowError for large inputs (e.g., factorialTail(100000, 1)). The tail-recursive style is still valuable for clarity and ease of conversion to iteration, but it does NOT give you performance or stack safety benefits in standard Java. To avoid stack overflow with large inputs, convert to an iterative loop explicitly.

sections.title: Head Recursion — Recursive Call First, Processing After

blocks.text: In head recursion, the recursive call is the first operation in the method — it recurses all the way down to the base case before any processing happens. All work (printing, computing) is done during the unwinding phase as stack frames pop. This means values are processed in reverse order compared to the input sequence.

blocks.label: HeadVsTailRecursion.java
lines: // HEAD RECURSION: recursive call FIRST, print during UNWINDING
// → prints numbers in REVERSE (from 1 up to n)
// (recurses to 0, then prints 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 on way back up)
// TAIL RECURSION: print FIRST, recursive call LAST
// → prints numbers in FORWARD order (from n down to 1)

blocks.title: 💡 Head vs Tail — Key Insight
blocks.text: Head recursion defers ALL work until the unwinding phase — the call stack winds all the way down first. This is why head recursion naturally reverses order. Tail recursion does work BEFORE the recursive call — during the winding phase. Understanding this distinction helps you predict output order in recursive methods and choose the right form when order matters.

sections.title: Tree Recursion — Multiple Recursive Calls Per Invocation

blocks.text: Tree recursion occurs when a method makes more than one recursive call per invocation, creating a branching call tree rather than a linear chain. The most classic example is the naive Fibonacci implementation. While elegant and easy to understand, naive tree recursion is often exponentially slow due to recalculating the same subproblems many times — a problem solved by memoization.

blocks.label: TreeRecursion.java
lines: // ❌ NAIVE Fibonacci — Tree Recursion — O(2^n) time, O(n) space
if (n <= 1) return n;                        // Base cases: fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1
return fibNaive(n - 1) + fibNaive(n - 2);   // TWO recursive calls — tree structure
//        ...         fib(2) is computed MULTIPLE TIMES → redundant work!
// ✅ Counting recursive calls — demonstrates exponential growth
// Tree recursion: Count ways to climb n stairs (1 or 2 steps at a time)
if (n == 1) return 1;     // Base case: one way to climb 1 step
if (n == 2) return 2;     // Base case: two ways (1+1, or 2)
return climbStairs(n - 1) + climbStairs(n - 2); // Two recursive calls

blocks.title: ⚠️ Tree Recursion — Exponential Time Without Memoization
blocks.text: Naive tree-recursive Fibonacci has O(2^n) time complexity — computing fib(50) requires over 2 trillion calls! fib(40) already takes several seconds on modern hardware. The problem is OVERLAPPING SUBPROBLEMS — fib(n-2) is recomputed in both the left and right subtrees. Solution: memoization (cache results, reuse them) converts O(2^n) to O(n). Always memoize tree-recursive functions with overlapping subproblems.

sections.title: Recursion vs Iteration — When to Use Which

blocks.text: Both recursion and iteration can solve the same class of problems — anything recursive can be rewritten iteratively using an explicit stack, and anything iterative can be rewritten recursively. However, choosing the right approach depends on problem structure, readability, performance requirements, and input size.

blocks.title: 💡 Rule of Thumb
blocks.text: Use recursion when: (1) The problem is inherently recursive in structure (trees, graphs, divide-and-conquer). (2) Code clarity and elegance outweigh performance concerns. (3) Input size is bounded and won't cause stack overflow. Use iteration when: (1) Input can be very large (millions of elements). (2) Performance and memory efficiency are critical. (3) The problem is a simple linear repetition with no branching structure. When in doubt, start with recursion for clarity, then optimize to iteration if needed.

sections.title: StackOverflowError — Causes, Detection, and Fixes

blocks.text: The StackOverflowError is the most common runtime error caused by recursion in Java. It occurs when the JVM's call stack runs out of memory because too many recursive calls have accumulated without returning. Each stack frame consumes memory (typically 100–200 bytes for a simple method) and the default JVM stack size is around 512KB, allowing roughly 2,000–10,000 frames before overflow occurs.

items.title: Cause 1: Missing Base Case
items.text: The most common cause — infinite recursion because the method never stops calling itself. Example: factorial(n) with no 'if (n==0) return 1' statement. The fix: always identify and implement the base case FIRST before writing the recursive case.

items.title: Cause 2: Base Case Unreachable
items.text: A base case exists but is never reached due to bad input or wrong logic. Example: factorial(-5) with base case 'if (n==0) return 1' — n counts down to -5, -6, -7... never reaching 0. Fix: validate input before recursing, or use a more inclusive base case like 'if (n <= 0) return 1'.

items.title: Cause 3: Input Too Large
items.text: The recursion is correct but the input is too deep for the JVM stack. Example: fibonacci(100000) would require 100,000 stack frames. Fix: (1) Convert to iteration. (2) Use memoization to reduce call depth. (3) Increase JVM stack size with -Xss flag (e.g., -Xss4m for 4MB).

items.title: Fix: Convert to Iteration
items.text: The safest fix for large-input recursion: convert to an iterative solution using a loop and explicit stack (java.util.Stack or Deque). This trades call-stack memory for heap memory, eliminating StackOverflowError. Most competitive and production Java code uses this approach for deep recursion.

sections.title: Memoization — Optimizing Recursive Solutions

blocks.text: Memoization is an optimization technique that stores the results of expensive recursive calls in a cache (usually a HashMap or array) and returns the cached result when the same inputs occur again. It is the key technique for transforming tree-recursive algorithms with overlapping subproblems from exponential time to linear time. Memoization is the top-down approach to Dynamic Programming.

sections.title: Bad Practices & Anti-Patterns — What Senior Developers Reject

blocks.text: These anti-patterns are common reasons for code review rejections and production bugs in Java codebases. Each either makes recursion unsafe, unmaintainable, or inefficient.

items.title: Using Recursion for Simple Iteration
items.text: Recursive methods for straightforward loops (summing an array, printing elements, finding max in a list) add unnecessary call-stack overhead and risk StackOverflowError for large collections. A simple for-loop or Java Streams is clearer, safer, and faster. Reserve recursion for inherently recursive structures (trees, graphs, divide-and-conquer).

items.title: Unguarded Recursion on Untrusted Input
items.text: Calling recursive methods on user-provided or external input without bounding the depth is a DoS vulnerability. Malicious or erroneous input (e.g., a deeply nested JSON, a cyclically-linked list passed as a tree) causes StackOverflowError. Always validate input size or depth before recursing, or use an explicit depth counter with a maximum.

items.title: Naive Tree Recursion Without Memoization
items.text: Writing fibNaive(n) or similar overlapping-subproblem functions without memoization is never acceptable beyond demonstration purposes. For any n > 40, it becomes unusable. Always memoize tree-recursive functions with overlapping subproblems, or convert to bottom-up dynamic programming.

items.title: Using Static/Instance Fields as Recursive State
items.text: Relying on static or instance variables to accumulate recursive results (static int count = 0) makes the method non-reentrant — calling it from multiple threads or calling it twice gives wrong results. Always use parameters or return values to pass state through recursion.

items.title: Deeply Recursive Methods in Web Request Handlers
items.text: In Spring Boot or servlet-based applications, each HTTP request runs on a thread pool thread with a fixed stack size. A deeply recursive method in a request handler can exhaust the thread's stack and crash the request handler. Use iterative implementations or configurable depth limits for recursive logic in web application code paths.

items.title: Ignoring Integer Overflow in Recursive Calculations
items.text: Recursive computations like factorial quickly exceed int range (overflow at 13!) or long range (overflow at 21!). Using int for factorial(20) silently returns wrong results. Use BigInteger for unbounded arithmetic: BigInteger factorial(int n) { if (n <= 1) return BigInteger.ONE; return factorial(n-1).multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(n)); }

sections.title: Java Recursion Interview Questions — Beginner to Advanced

blocks.text: These questions are consistently asked in Java developer interviews, data structures & algorithms rounds, and FAANG-style technical screenings.

items.q: Q1. What is recursion in Java? What are its essential components?
items.a: Recursion in Java is a technique where a method calls itself to solve a problem by reducing it into smaller subproblems of the same type. Three essential components: (1) BASE CASE — a condition that terminates recursion and returns a value directly without further calling. (2) RECURSIVE CASE — the method calls itself with a modified (smaller/simpler) argument. (3) PROGRESS/CONVERGENCE — each recursive call must move closer to the base case. Without a base case: StackOverflowError. Without progress: StackOverflowError even with a base case. Without a recursive case: it's just a regular method, not recursive.

items.q: Q2. What is the difference between recursion and iteration?
items.a: Recursion calls itself, uses call stack for state, and is natural for inherently recursive structures (trees, graphs). Iteration uses loops, uses constant stack space, and is efficient for linear repetition. Recursion: O(n) stack space, method call overhead, risk of StackOverflowError for deep inputs, more elegant for recursive structures. Iteration: O(1) stack space, no call overhead, safer for large inputs, more verbose for tree/graph algorithms. Both are equally powerful (Turing equivalent) — anything recursive can be iterative and vice versa. Rule: use recursion when problem structure IS recursive; use iteration otherwise.

items.q: Q3. Write a recursive method to compute the nth Fibonacci number.
items.a: public static long fib(int n) { if (n < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException(); if (n <= 1) return n; return fib(n-1) + fib(n-2); } — Two base cases: fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1. This is tree recursion with O(2^n) complexity. For interviews, also mention the memoized version: use a HashMap or array to cache results, achieving O(n) time. For very large n, mention the bottom-up iterative O(n)/O(1) solution. Interviewers expect you to identify the time complexity issue with naive recursion and offer optimization.

items.q: Q4. What is StackOverflowError in Java? When does recursion cause it?
items.a: StackOverflowError is thrown by the JVM when the call stack runs out of memory from too many nested method calls. Each recursive call creates a stack frame (holds parameters, local vars, return address). JVM default stack: ~512KB–1MB ≈ 1,000–10,000 frames. Causes: (1) No base case — infinite recursion. (2) Base case unreachable — e.g., factorial(-1) with base case n==0. (3) Input too large — correct recursion but too deep. Fixes: add/fix base case, validate input, convert to iteration, increase stack size with JVM flag -Xss. Unlike Java heap errors (OutOfMemoryError), StackOverflowError cannot be recovered from gracefully in most cases.

items.q: Q5. What is tail recursion? Does Java optimize it?
items.a: Tail recursion is when the recursive call is the LAST operation in the method — no computation happens after it returns. To achieve this, intermediate results are passed as accumulator parameters. Example: factorialTail(n, acc) where acc builds the product. IMPORTANT: The standard Java JVM (HotSpot) does NOT perform Tail Call Optimization (TCO). This is a deliberate choice — Java preserves full stack traces for debugging. So tail-recursive Java methods can still cause StackOverflowError for large n. Languages like Scala (which runs on JVM) and Kotlin support TCO via @tailrec annotation. In Java, manually convert tail recursion to iteration for stack safety.

items.q: Q6. What is memoization and how does it optimize recursion?
items.a: Memoization is caching the result of a recursive call so that if the same inputs occur again, the cached result is returned instead of recomputing. It converts tree-recursive algorithms with overlapping subproblems from exponential to linear time. Implementation: use a HashMap<Integer, Long> or int[] array as cache. Before computing, check if cache contains the key — if yes, return cached value. After computing, store the result in cache. Classic example: memoizing Fibonacci converts O(2^n) to O(n). Memoization is the top-down approach to Dynamic Programming. Bottom-up DP (tabulation) fills the cache from the smallest subproblem up, often avoiding recursion entirely.

items.q: Q7. What is the difference between direct and indirect recursion?
items.a: Direct recursion: method A calls itself — A → A → A → base case. Simple, clear, easy to trace. Most recursion is direct. Indirect (mutual) recursion: method A calls method B, which calls method A — A → B → A → B → ... → base case. Each method in the cycle must have a path to a base case. Used in parsers, grammar evaluators, and state machines. Harder to trace and debug. Java has no syntactic restriction on either form — both compile identically. For indirect recursion, ensure BOTH methods have appropriate base cases and that the cycle always terminates.

items.q: Q8. How would you solve the Tower of Hanoi recursively? What is its time complexity?
items.a: hanoi(n, src, dst, aux): Base case: if (n==1) print 'Move disc 1 from src to dst'. Recursive: (1) Move n-1 discs from src to aux (using dst as auxiliary). (2) Move disc n from src to dst. (3) Move n-1 discs from aux to dst (using src as auxiliary). Time complexity: T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1, which solves to O(2^n) — minimum possible moves is 2^n - 1. Space complexity: O(n) for the call stack. Tower of Hanoi is significant because it's a problem that CANNOT be solved in less than O(2^n) moves — the recursive solution is optimal. It perfectly demonstrates recursive problem decomposition: solve n-1 discs twice plus one move.

items.q: Q9. How do you convert a recursive solution to an iterative one?
items.a: General approach: replace the call stack with an explicit java.util.Deque (ArrayDeque). (1) Push the initial state onto the deque. (2) Loop while deque is not empty: pop a state, process it, push child states. For tail recursion specifically: just convert to a while loop with the accumulator as a loop variable. Example — recursive DFS becomes iterative DFS by replacing the call stack with an explicit Stack<Node>. Benefits of iterative conversion: no StackOverflowError risk, better performance (no method call overhead), configurable memory allocation on heap. Tradeoff: more code, explicit state management.

items.q: Q10. What is the time and space complexity of recursive Fibonacci (naive) and how do you optimize it?
items.a: Naive recursive Fibonacci: T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + O(1) → Time: O(2^n), Space: O(n) call stack. fib(50) requires over 2 trillion calls. Three optimizations: (1) Memoization (top-down DP): cache results in HashMap/array — Time: O(n), Space: O(n). (2) Tabulation (bottom-up DP): fill array from fib[0] to fib[n] iteratively — Time: O(n), Space: O(n). (3) Space-optimized iteration: only track prev and curr — Time: O(n), Space: O(1). (4) Matrix exponentiation: Time: O(log n). For interviews, explain all approaches and their tradeoffs. The naive solution demonstrates overlapping subproblems; memoization demonstrates dynamic programming thinking.

sections.title: Practice Questions — Test Your Recursion Knowledge

blocks.text: Attempt each question independently before reading the answer. For recursion, always trace through a small example by hand — writing out the call stack is the most effective way to build intuition.

items.a: Output: 15. This is the sum of integers from 1 to 5: 5+4+3+2+1+0 = 15. Trace: mystery(5) = 5 + mystery(4) = 5 + 4 + mystery(3) = 5+4+3+2+1+0 = 15. Base case: mystery(0) = 0. Each call adds n to the sum of all smaller integers.

Bug: Missing base case → infinite recursion → StackOverflowError. countdown(n-1) is called forever. Fix: public static void countdown(int n) { if (n < 0) return; // Base case System.out.println(n); countdown(n - 1); } — also note the return type should be void since we never return a value. The base case stops recursion when n goes below 0.

items.q: 3. Write a recursive method to check if a string is a palindrome.
items.a: public static boolean isPalindrome(String s) { if (s.length() <= 1) return true; // Base case: 0 or 1 chars are palindromes if (s.charAt(0) != s.charAt(s.length() - 1)) return false; // Mismatch return isPalindrome(s.substring(1, s.length() - 1)); // Check inner substring } // isPalindrome('racecar') → 'r'=='r', check 'aceca' → 'a'=='a', check 'cec' → 'c'=='c', check 'e' → true. isPalindrome('hello') → 'h'!='o' → false.

Time complexity: O(2^n) — exponential. Each call spawns two calls, creating a binary tree of depth n with 2^n leaves. fib(40) makes ~330 million calls; fib(50) makes ~2 trillion. Improvement — memoization: private static long[] memo = new long[100]; public static long fib(int n) { if (n <= 1) return n; if (memo[n] != 0) return memo[n]; return memo[n] = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2); } — This reduces time to O(n) by caching and reusing computed values instead of recomputing them in overlapping subtrees.

Output: 1 2 3 4 5. This is HEAD recursion — the recursive call happens FIRST, then printing happens during unwinding. The method recurses all the way down to print(0) (base case), then prints 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 as the stack unwinds. If print were: System.out.print(n + ' '); then print(n-1) — that would be TAIL recursion and print 5 4 3 2 1.

items.q: 6. Write a recursive method to compute the sum of all digits of a number. sumDigits(12345) should return 15.
items.a: public static int sumDigits(int n) { if (n < 0) return sumDigits(-n); // Handle negatives if (n < 10) return n; // Base case: single digit return (n % 10) + sumDigits(n / 10); // Last digit + sum of remaining digits } // Trace for sumDigits(12345): (5) + sumDigits(1234) → (5+4) + sumDigits(123) → (5+4+3) + sumDigits(12) → (5+4+3+2) + sumDigits(1) → (5+4+3+2+1) = 15

public static long factorialIterative(int n) { if (n < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("n must be >= 0"); long result = 1; for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) { result *= i; } return result; } — This is equivalent to the recursive version but uses O(1) stack space instead of O(n) stack frames. No risk of StackOverflowError for any valid int input (though overflow occurs for n > 20 with long). For n = 0 or 1, the loop doesn't execute and result remains 1.

Bug: The recursive case calls power(base, exp) with the SAME exp — it never decreases! This is infinite recursion → StackOverflowError. The base case (exp==0) will never be reached because exp never changes. Fix: return base * power(base, exp - 1); — exp must decrease by 1 each call. Also: this doesn't handle negative exponents. Improved fix: public static double power(double base, int exp) { if (exp == 0) return 1; if (exp < 0) return 1.0 / power(base, -exp); return base * power(base, exp - 1); }

sections.title: Conclusion — Recursion: The Art of Solving Problems with Themselves

blocks.text: Recursion is one of the most elegant and powerful concepts in programming. At its core, it is the art of defining a solution in terms of itself — breaking a complex problem into a simpler version of the same problem until you reach a case simple enough to answer directly. Once you internalize this thinking, you will see recursive structure everywhere: in file systems, in JSON/XML data, in binary trees, in organizational hierarchies, in sorting algorithms.

The difference between a developer who understands recursion and one who merely knows it is visible in practice. Beginners write recursion that works for happy-path inputs but crashes on negative values, large inputs, or null data. Experienced developers write recursive methods with input validation, clear base cases, bounded depth, memoization for overlapping subproblems, and awareness of when iteration is the better choice.

items.q: What is recursion in Java?
items.a: Recursion in Java is a programming technique where a method calls itself directly or indirectly to solve a problem by breaking it into smaller subproblems of the same type. Every recursive method must have a base case (where recursion stops and a direct value is returned) and a recursive case (where the method calls itself with a modified argument moving toward the base case). Without a base case, recursion continues infinitely and causes a StackOverflowError.

items.q: What is the difference between recursion and iteration in Java?
items.a: Recursion uses method self-calls and the call stack to maintain state, consuming O(n) stack memory and risking StackOverflowError for large inputs. Iteration uses loops and consumes O(1) stack space with no overflow risk. Recursion is more natural for tree/graph structures and divide-and-conquer algorithms; iteration is more efficient for simple linear repetition. Both are equally powerful — use recursion for recursive structures and iteration for linear tasks.

items.q: What is a base case in recursion?
items.a: A base case is the condition in a recursive method that stops further recursive calls and returns a direct result. Every correct recursive method needs at least one base case. Without it, the method recurses infinitely until a StackOverflowError terminates the program. The base case must be reachable — every possible input must eventually lead to the base case through successive recursive calls.

items.q: What is tail recursion in Java?
items.a: Tail recursion is when the recursive call is the last operation in the method — no computation is pending after it returns. Intermediate results are passed as accumulator parameters. While theoretically optimizable, the Java JVM does NOT perform tail call optimization. Tail-recursive Java methods still create new stack frames and can cause StackOverflowError for large inputs. Convert to explicit iteration for stack safety with large inputs.

items.q: What causes StackOverflowError in Java recursion?
items.a: StackOverflowError occurs when the JVM call stack runs out of memory from too many nested recursive calls. Common causes: (1) Missing base case — infinite recursion. (2) Base case unreachable — e.g., negative input with base case at zero. (3) Input too large — correct logic but exceeds stack capacity (typically 1,000–10,000 frames). Fixes: add or fix the base case, validate inputs before recursing, convert to iteration, or increase stack size with the JVM flag -Xss.
